 "They used all my benefits." Within minutes of it reaching her account, one Phoenix mom's grocery budget was stolen. 
 By Sara Crocker November 2, 2026 
 Carla Brambila's SNAP benefits were stolen in October. Provided by Carla Brambila

 This article is part of a package of stories featured on this week’s cover, exploring the devastating fallout Arizona has seen after the federal government gutted food assistance last year. The cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, SNAP, have left Arizonans making hard decisions to feed their families. 
 Carla Brambila is an early riser. The mom of five checks her SNAP account just after 5 a.m. on the day the money posts each month. 
 She has been on disability since a devastating car accident in 2019 broke her spine. Though she was bedridden and then used a wheelchair, she’s learned to walk again and manage her pain while raising her children, who range in age from 8 months to 14 years old. 
 A single, stay-at-home mom, Brambila lives in a two-bedroom Phoenix apartment with her mom, kids and nephew.

 SNAP cuts leave Arizonans making hard decisions to feed their families 
 Over 770,000 children no longer receive SNAP after Trump changes food program 
 SNAP work requirements don’t help people get jobs. They prevent getting food 
 Each month, the 32-year-old receives $1,023 from SNAP, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. 
 The federal program has helped low-income families bolster their grocery budgets for nearly 90 years. Today, people receive these extra dollars on debit-like cards to use at grocery stores and farmers markets.
 This month, Brambila planned to buy ingredients to make tamales and soups for her kids, and her 5-year-old’s favorite apple juice. 
 When she logged in to check her account on Oct. 4, she was shocked by what she saw.
 advertisement 
 advertisement 
 “Somebody used my card to order online,” she says, “and they used all my benefits.”
 She had just $3 left in her account; the other $1,020 had been wiped out. She suspects someone stole her card information, which she’s heard of happening to people she knows, including her sister.
 The federal government overhauled SNAP last summer, adding new work requirements and pushing more costs onto states. Proponents have touted the changes as necessary to weed out fraud and trim a bloated system to serve only those who need food assistance the most.
 By the government’s own estimates, intentional fraud to game the system accounts for less than 1% of all benefits, or about $64 million. Unintentional errors, under- or overpaying benefits, are more common.
 advertisement 
 Yet changes to SNAP to address that fraud have led to a 52% drop in the number of people receiving benefits in Arizona, which is the steepest decline in the nation. 
 That huge drop-off didn’t come from eradicating fraud. Instead, people trying to get or stay on SNAP were met with unanswered calls and more onerous documentation requests. The changes left many without benefits not because they didn’t qualify, but because of technicalities.
 The government’s efforts to squash fraud have instead left many families going hungry. The fraud, like what happened to Brambila, remains. 
 During the recent upheaval, Brambila was able to keep her SNAP benefits. But this month, she was still left with no money to buy food.
 advertisement 
 advertisement 
 SNAP is disbursed via debit-like cards, which lack chips. 
 U.S. Department of Agriculture
 How does SNAP theft happen? 
 Criminals have targeted the food stamp program for years because of its outdated safeguards, which are easy to bypass. 
 SNAP cards only have a magnetic strip. They lack the modern microchips embedded in credit or debit cards. Thieves skim these cards, often by attaching a device to a card reader to steal the card number and other information, and then clone them.
 advertisement 
 The federal government knows this is a problem. In the last two years, $233 million in SNAP benefits may have been lost to this kind of theft, a report by the Department of Agriculture’s Office of Inspector General found. A ProPublica investigation suggests the theft could be more widespread, estimating $470 million was stolen electronically from beneficiaries in 2025. 
 Eight states currently use microchipped cards and another six are part of a government pilot program. That technology has not yet expanded to Arizona. 
 Meanwhile, Arizonans dealing with theft, like Brambila, are left with few options. After noticing just $3 in her account, she went to the Arizona Department of Economic Security, which administers SNAP, as soon as the office opened. DES gave her a new SNAP card, but wouldn’t restore the money she lost for the month, she says. 
 There would be no tamales or apple juice in October. 
 advertisement 
 advertisement 
 While the federal government left her empty-handed, Brambila turned to local nonprofits to feed her family. She visited two food pantries and relied on nightly dinners served at the Society of St. Vincent de Paul in South Phoenix.   
 Normally, her kids get breakfast and lunch at school. But just after she discovered her SNAP account had been drained, her kids’ schools sent students home for fall break.
 They ate most of the fruit, vegetables, bread and canned goods from the food pantries that week.
 For now, Brambila’s mom has shouldered the extra bills. Brambila calls her mom her “backbone,” adding, “she helps a lot.” That included buying about $150 in groceries for the family last week, which Brambila knows is not sustainable. 
 “It’s just really difficult. I wish the government could do better,” Brambila says. “They know we struggle, but they don’t want to provide more help for us. ”

 Sara Crocker is a staff writer for Phoenix New Times where she focuses primarily on food. She began freelancing for New Times in July 2022 and joined the staff in February 2023. Prior to New Times , Sara worked for publications such as The Denver Post , Phoenix Magazine , Phoenix Home & Garden and Colorado Life Magazine . When she’s not reporting on the Valley’s dining scene, Sara brews beer at home and is an avid cook.
